In nineteen seventy-nine, a Navy jail in Seattle let a researcher try something strange.
He swore one color could switch off violence.
The recipe? One pint of red. One gallon of white. He called it P six eighteen.
So the two men running the jail, Baker and Miller, painted their confinement cells bubblegum pink.
Angry men went in. After about fifteen minutes, the Navy reported, the fight was gone.
The color took their names, and the story took off.
Jails. Police stations. A football coach even painted the visitors' locker room.
By twenty fifteen, one in five Swiss lockups had a pink cell.
But a California jail looked closer. Fifteen minutes? Calm. Twenty minutes? It flipped.
Then, in twenty fourteen, scientists put fifty-nine prisoners in pink or gray rooms for three days.
Aggression dropped in both. The color made no difference.
All that paint, and the walls may never have done a thing.
